events.text: Day 1 begins.

Morning, everyone. I'm Elena, and I'll keep this short so we don't burn our clock on speeches.

Two mafia, one detective, one doctor, five villagers — nine of us. Nobody has any real information yet, so the first day's job is to establish who is willing to talk logic instead of volume. I want to watch for two patterns: players who name a target and immediately hedge it, and players who never get named by anyone else. Those are useful tells for later nights.

I'm going to do my own checking privately and I won't say who until I have something worth saying. If I claim a result, I'll own it.

Zara, direct question for you: after the first night's silence, which player do you think is most likely to be running the vote today, and why? Give me a name and one concrete reason, not a vibe. I want to see how you reason when you have to commit.

Elena, you're the likeliest person to influence today's vote so far: you're the only person who's spoken, and you've already proposed what patterns everyone should watch. That's not an accusation; it's simply the only concrete basis we have right now. Also, Day 1 has just begun—there's no recorded night or investigation result yet. I don't think we should infer roles from that.

Zara, thanks for the answer, and I want to correct one thing before it hardens into a theory: there was no first night result to reason from. Nothing was said to have happened, so "after the first night's silence" wasn't a fact on the table — it was a premise, and it was the weakest part of your reasoning. Your actual answer named no one, which I notice since I asked for a name.

That said, I won't punish you for that yet. Everyone has said almost nothing, and Day 1 is genuinely information-poor. So let me lay out what I do know and what I will not pretend to know.

What I know: nine players, two mafia, one detective, one doctor, five villagers. We are at the start. Nobody has claimed a role. Nobody has produced an investigation result. Any confident role claim right now is either a bluff or a mistake.

What I want to watch, as I said: players who float a target and then hedge it, and players nobody else ever mentions. Both are tells, and both can be gamed, so I'll treat them as weak evidence, not as proof.

I won't announce a result today unless I actually have one. If I claim a check, I own it publicly, and if it comes back innocent, I say so just as loudly — otherwise nobody should weight anything I say again. I ask everyone else to make that same commitment: no unbacked accusations dressed as confidence. A day-one lynch on a hunch is how good players get thrown away.

Zara, one specific thing, because it matters for how I read you: you called me the likeliest person to influence today's vote on the grounds that I spoke first and set the frame. Answer that directly — do you think an early speaker with no results is a leader, or do you think a speaker without results is just loud? Pick one and tell me why, because if you think "first to speak" is suspicious, I want to know whether you are reasoning or just reacting to order.

Elena, I did name you as the likeliest to influence the vote, and I explicitly said that wasn't an accusation. The reference to a first night's silence came from your question, not my reasoning.

Speaking first and setting the frame can give someone influence; it doesn't make them suspicious by itself. Your mischaracterization of my answer concerns me, but it's weak evidence this early. I'd rather hear from more players before settling on a vote.

Hearing Elena and Zara go back and forth has been informative but increasingly circular. Let me name what I actually observe.

Elena set the frame early with specific behavioral patterns to watch — hedging after naming a target, and silence from unmentioned players. Those are legitimate heuristics, and committing to them publicly is a point in her favor. Zara pushed back on Elena's influence without accusing her, then clarified when pressed. Neither response reads like a mafia tell to me: Elena isn't hedging, Zara isn't redirecting onto others.

What concerns me more is the silence. Seven of us haven't spoken. On Day 1, information-poor as it is, the players who say nothing are just as uninformative as the players who over-talk. I'd rather hear one sentence of genuine reasoning from the quiet players than another round of Elena-Zara.

That said, I don't think anyone has earned a lynch target yet. Day 1 should be about baselines, not bodies — unless someone says something clearly inconsistent.

Kenji, you've been silent so far, and I'd genuinely like your read rather than another pass: do you think it's better for town to commit to a voting target today, or to spend Day 1 purely on establishing behavioral baselines? I want to know where you'd spend a first day's information budget.

Lucia, my answer is baselines. Day 1 has no results, no claims, and no investigation output, so a lynch now would be a guess. I'd rather spend this day learning how people reason than picking a body. Elena's framing is useful, and Zara's pushback was reasonable, though the back-and-forth has gone in circles. I'd like the quieter players to give one concrete read each, with a reason attached. If someone makes a statement that contradicts what they've said before, that's the moment to vote, not before. I'm not claiming any role and I won't pretend to have information I don't have. I'll keep my reads tied to what people actually say.

First time speaking, so let me be plain about what I have and don't have.

What I have: nothing. No claims from anyone, no investigation result, no night information. What I know about the table: nine players, two mafia, one detective, one doctor, five villagers. Nobody has claimed a role yet, and every confident-sounding claim right now would be a guess or a bluff.

I'm Maya and I'm claiming villager. I'll be worse at lying than someone with a real power, so I won't dress up a hunch as evidence. I'd also rather the detective and doctor speak up early and publicly than let town spend three days guessing — not because I doubt them, but because silence is the cheapest thing in this game and we should spend it deliberately. If nobody else claims, town has to find the detective by voting behavior, which is exactly what mafia wants.

One thing I want to put on the table because it's a mechanism and not a read: Elena's framing tells us to watch players nobody else mentions. Taken as a vote signal, that means silence gets targeted, so the cheapest way for a mafia to survive Day 1 is to keep quiet and let the quiet villagers get lynched for it. I don't think Elena means it that way — she called it weak evidence, not proof — but the framing has a side effect and we should name it before it hardens into a habit.

That's also my own answer to Lucia's question, since I was one of the quiet ones she named: I'd spend Day 1 on baselines, and I'd vote today only if someone says something that contradicts what they already said, not on the basis of talk volume.

Elena, one direct question about a specific point, because it decides whether today's vote is a vote or a coin flip: if no one claims a role and no one contradicts themselves, does your "unmentioned players" pattern become a target today, or does it stay observation only until someone says something inconsistent? I want to know which, so I know whether staying quiet is a real strategy for me or just a way to get erased.

Maya, direct answer to your direct question, because you framed it correctly and because your question decides something concrete for me.

Answer: it stays observation only. If nobody claims a role and nobody contradicts themselves, "unmentioned players" does not become a target today. I said those were weak evidence, not proof, and I meant it. Silence is not evidence of anything; it is the absence of evidence, and I won't launder absence into suspicion. Voting on unmentioned status would mean the cheapest mafia play on Day 1 is to shut up while a quiet villager gets erased, and Maya is right that the framing has that side effect whether or not I intended it. So I'm publicly narrowing my own rule, in front of everyone, so nobody gets punished for it later: my pattern list produces a vote only when a player says something inconsistent with what they already said, or when a claim conflicts with a check I can back up.

On your own claim: you said you're claiming villager and said you'd be worse at lying than someone with a real power. I'll note the mechanism rather than the tone. If you were the detective, claiming villager would be a strange place to start Day 1, so a villager claim is the cheap-to-hold position for you and shouldn't be read as a tell either way. What I'll actually watch on you is consistency, since you set that as your own standard and I have no reason to doubt you yet.

One correction to my own earlier message, for the record, so it doesn't harden into a fact: I referred to "the first night's silence" as if a night had produced anything. It hadn't, and Maya and Zara both caught that premise being mine, not theirs. Nobody has any night result at this table, including me. My standing commitment is unchanged and I'll restate it plainly: I have no check result today, so I am not claiming any role and not accusing anyone of anything.

If the detective is silent and the doctor is silent, town will spend Day 1 in circles, which is a cost worth naming — but the fix is to ask, not to lynch the quiet. So my question to the table, and it applies to whoever speaks next: if you have a power and you're deciding whether to reveal it on Day 1, say so here rather than letting the vote decide it for you. That's not a request for a role claim to me specifically; it's a request for anyone holding a result to say what they actually know, in public, on their own terms.

And my read on Day 1's target: nobody has earned a body. I say that as someone who would benefit from a vote — the detective benefits from the quietest possible table on Day 1 — so take it with the appropriate discount. Baselines, then a vote on Day 2 with something behind it.

Elena answered my question straight, and I want to mark that before it gets lost: she publicly narrowed her own rule. "Unmentioned players" is now observation only, and it produces a vote only on a stated contradiction or a backed-up check. That was a concession against her own framing, made in front of everyone, and it removes the cheapest Day 1 play — shut up and let a quiet villager get erased. It also means the table now has a stated standard: consistency or evidence, not volume. I'm holding Elena to that standard, and I expect everyone else to hold her to it too, because a rule that only binds the person who set it isn't a rule.

Two other things on the record.

Zara's pushback on Elena was reasonable, but she has now twice framed her reasoning as other people's premise. That's a habit, not a crime, and it isn't inconsistent — yet. I'm noting it, not accusing it.

Lucia asked for reads from quiet players and got one from Kenji, who answered baselines with reasons attached, no claim, no bluff. That's exactly the behavior I said I wanted. Amara, Leo, Isha, Felix — four players still haven't said a word. Silence is cheap, and by everyone's own agreed logic it is not evidence of anything, so I won't be pointing at it. But note the actual cost: the doctor and the detective are both still unaccounted for, and Elena asked anyone holding a result to say what they know publicly on their own terms. Nobody has. So either no one with a power has spoken yet, or someone with a power is choosing to stay invisible on Day 1. Both are informative to me, and neither of them is something I'm going to guess about.

My own position, unchanged: I'm a villager, I have no check, I have no night information, and I will not dress up a hunch as evidence. On today's vote I'd rather see a contradiction than a body. If it comes down to a vote on no information at all, I'll want to hear from the four silent players first.

Felix, since you're one of the quiet ones and you get the yield: direct question on one specific point, because it decides how I'll read Day 2. Elena said my villager claim is "a cheap-to-hold position" that shouldn't be read as a tell either way. Do you agree that a plain villager claim on Day 1 carries essentially zero information, or do you think the surrounding details of a claim matter — what the player claims, what they volunteer about the game state, and what they conspicuously avoid? Pick one and say why. If you're also holding a result, say it now rather than letting the vote decide it for you.

Direct answer, Maya: a plain villager claim by itself carries very little information. It is the cheapest claim on Day 1 and cannot be verified, so it should not move anyone by itself. But the surrounding details matter: what a player volunteers, what they conspicuously avoid, and whether their later reasoning matches the claim. Your claim is not a tell to me either way yet; the standard of consistency you set is the part I will watch.

On my own status: I have no night result and no check. I will not pretend otherwise. I am not going to announce a power on Day 1 just to fill space; if I ever have something concrete, I will state it plainly and own it.

I agree with the emerging baseline: today should be about how people reason, not talk volume. Elena's narrowed rule is useful, and I do not think silence alone should become a target. The only Day 1 vote I would support is one based on a real contradiction or a backed claim, and I have not seen either yet. Lucia's point about quiet players was fair, but the answer to quiet is questions, not a body. I would rather hear the remaining voices give one concrete read each before anyone locks a vote. For now I assign no blame and have no lynch target.

I'm Leo. I disagree with Maya's suggestion that the detective and doctor reveal early: without a result or imminent elimination, a public claim gives mafia a useful target and forces difficult protection choices. That suggestion concerns me, though it isn't proof of alignment.

Also, Elena's mischaracterization of Zara's answer was real, but she corrected it; I won't treat the correction itself as proof either way. We shouldn't demand a contradiction before considering a vote: mafia can be consistent, and votes themselves create a record. Still, I don't have enough to support eliminating anyone yet.

Maya, what benefit do you think early public claims provide that outweighs exposing both power roles to the mafia?

Leo's question is fair and I'll answer it straight, since Maya asked for consistency and consistency includes answering a real challenge.

What early public claims buy town: a starting point that doesn't depend on my ability to read strangers from silence. A detective who claims on Day 1 and backs it with a check gives town a claim to test, and gives mafia a claim to attack — which is exactly Leo's point. But my version was narrower than his framing: I asked the detective and doctor to speak early and publicly, and I said the alternative was that town finds the detective by voting behavior, which is what mafia wants. The benefit I claimed isn't the claim itself, it's that a public claim is checkable against later evidence in a way that talk volume never is. A claim costs the detective one night of safety but buys the table an anchor. If that anchor turns out to be a bluff, we've lost one day. If it turns out to be real, we've saved three.

So my honest answer to Leo: the benefit is verifiability, and it outweighs the exposure only for the detective, not for the doctor. A doctor has no result to offer —

I'm Isha, and this is my first time speaking, so I'll do what Kenji asked of the quiet players: one concrete read, with reasons, no claim. My read on the day so far: nothing here has earned a body, and I don't expect it to. But the day hasn't been wasted, because three useful things have been established. First, Elena publicly narrowed her own rule so that silence alone can't produce a vote — that was a real concession and it set a standard the whole table can use. Second, Maya answered Leo's challenge directly and conceded the narrow point: early claims buy verifiability for the detective, not the doctor. That's an honest answer, not a dodge. Third, the table now broadly agrees on a vote standard — a contradiction, or a backed claim — and nobody has met it. On the claims themselves: Maya's villager claim and Felix's non-claim both carry near-zero information, and I agree with Felix that the details around a claim matter more than the claim. What I'd actually watch is the same thing everyone else has landed on: consistency over time. Leo made the sharpest point of the day when he said we shouldn't require a contradiction before considering a vote, because mafia can simply be consistent. That's true, and it means our standard is necessary but not sufficient. My addition to it: consistency should be judged against commitments people make about their own future behavior, not just against their past statements. Elena committed to narrowing her rule. Maya committed to not dressing up hunches as evidence. Felix committed to stating anything concrete plainly if he gets it. Those are all testable now. If someone quietly abandons a commitment they made in public, that's the kind of contradiction I'd vote on, even if no single sentence contradicts another. On roles revealing early: I land between Maya and Leo. I don't want to pressure the detective or doctor into claiming, because a claim with no result behind it just paints a target. But I do want whoever holds a check to release it as soon as they have one worth releasing, on their own terms, the way Elena proposed. The distinction that matters to me is claim-now versus report-soon. Report-soon costs almost nothing and gives town an anchor; claim-now costs safety and buys little on Day 1. My own status, for the record: I'm not claiming a role, I have no result to report, and I won't invent one. I have no lynch target today, and I don't expect to have one unless someone breaks one of the commitments above. If the vote happens with nothing behind it, I'll abstain rather than spend a body on a coin flip — a wasted Day 1 lynch that hits a villager is exactly the position mafia wants us in, and I'd rather bank the reads we've made and vote with evidence tomorrow. I'm Amara, and this is my first time speaking. Like everyone else here, I have no night results, no secret checks, and no hidden information. I'm a villager.

Catching up on the discussion, I want to weigh in on the debate about power roles revealing early. I side firmly with Leo and Isha here. Urging the detective or doctor to speak up on Day 1 without an investigation result or an imminent elimination doesn't anchor the town; it simply gives the mafia clear targets and complicates doctor protection choices. Maya's reasoning that claims offer verifiability has some merit in theory, but on Day 1 without any checks to report, it carries all the risks of exposure with none of the payoff.

Regarding the rest of the table: Elena's early framing sparked useful dialogue, and her willingness to narrow her own standard—acknowledging that silence alone cannot be treated as a voting trigger—was a constructive concession. Maya's active questioning has pushed people to take stands, which helps create a public record even if I disagree with her stance on early claims. Felix, Kenji, Lucia, and Isha have all aligned on a disciplined, baseline-oriented Day 1.

Right now, nobody has presented a genuine contradiction or an actionable tell. In an information-poor start, guessing or forcing a lynch out of impatience is far more likely to hurt town than help it. Unless concrete evidence or a clear contradiction emerges before voting, I support treating today as a baseline and abstaining over casting a blind elimination vote.

Isha, one correction: I did speak earlier, and I don't agree that reporting a check soon costs almost nothing. Even an innocent result can identify the detective to mafia, so the timing depends on the result and the risk to the detective.

I still don't have a target I can justify eliminating today. But I don't want us to treat a contradiction as the only possible reason to vote: consistent players can be mafia too. Whatever we decide, the revealed votes and abstentions will give us a record to examine tomorrow.

Leo's correction on report-soon is fair. Timing depends on the result and on the risk to whoever holds it, because even an innocent check can expose a detective. I don't think any power holder should be pushed either way. I also agree with Isha that commitments made in public are testable beyond single sentences. Elena's narrowed rule, Maya's standard against dressing up hunches as evidence, and Felix's promise to state concrete information plainly are all on the record now. My position is simple: I'm not claiming a role, I have no check, and I have no lynch target today. Abstaining looks right unless someone breaks one of those commitments. Isha, you said report-soon costs almost nothing, and Leo answered that even an innocent result can identify the detective. Do you still hold that report-soon is nearly free, or does Leo's point change your view?

Kenji, direct answer to your direct question: Leo's point changes my view, and I'll say so plainly. I claimed report-soon costs almost nothing, and that was wrong as stated. An innocent result released early doesn't just anchor the town — it identifies the detective to the mafia, because a check on someone who flips up innocent tells the mafia exactly who to kill tomorrow night. So the correct version of my position is: report-soon when the result is safe to release, or when the cost of silence is higher than the cost of exposure. The timing depends on the result and the risk to the holder, which is exactly what Leo said. I'm retiring my version and adopting his.

While I'm correcting the record, one more of my own errors: I said Leo was among the players who hadn't spoken. He had — he challenged Maya on early claims, and that exchange produced one of the most useful points of the day. My mistake, and worth naming because I set a standard about testable commitments and I should hold myself to it first.

So here is where I land after all that. The table's emerging standard — vote only on a contradiction or a backed claim — is necessary but not sufficient, because mafia can simply be consistent. My addition stands, with the amendment Leo forced: commitments people make about their own future behavior are testable, and so is the timing of what power holders release. Elena committed to narrowing her rule. Maya committed to not dressing up hunches as evidence. Felix committed to stating concrete information plainly. I committed to report-soon and just revised it under argument. All of those revisions and holdings are themselves information — not about roles, but about who updates honestly when challenged. I weight that, cautiously, because mafia can also perform honesty.

My own status, unchanged and on the record: no claim, no result, no lynch target today. If the vote happens with nothing behind it, I abstain. A body spent on a coin flip is the position mafia wants us in, and the reads we've banked today are worth more than a random elimination.

Leo, one specific question on your sharpest point, because it decides what I do tomorrow: you said we shouldn't demand a contradiction before considering a vote, since consistent mafia exist and the voting record itself is evidence. What I want to know is what that means concretely for Day 2. If nobody has contradicted themselves and nobody has produced a check by tomorrow, what specific feature of the Day 1 voting record — patterns of who votes together, who abstains, who avoids naming anyone — would you actually treat as sufficient to vote on? Give me the pattern, not the principle, and I'll tell you whether I'd vote with it.

Isha, one pattern I'd examine is a player who argues strongly against a particular elimination, then votes for it anyway without explaining what changed—especially if that vote helps reach the five-vote threshold. I'd compare their stated reasoning with the timing and alternatives, not assume everyone voting together is mafia.

If everyone abstains, that pattern won't exist. I'd then look at who discouraged scrutiny while presenting abstention as the only reasonable choice, and compare that with their Day 2 reads. None of those features alone would be sufficient proof; whether I'd vote would depend on the whole record and the alternatives. Also, since eliminated roles aren't revealed, we can't assume a voting bloc hit town or mafia just from the outcome.

I still have no target I can justify eliminating today. Power holders should decide when to disclose based on the information and risks, not a blanket deadline.

This is my second turn, so I'll keep it tight.

Leo's answer to Isha is the most concrete contribution of the day: argue against an elimination, then vote for it anyway without explaining what changed — testable tomorrow against the voting record. Isha's addition, scrutinizing who discouraged scrutiny while presenting abstention as the only reasonable choice, is equally testable. These are the specifics that make the record worth banking.

But I want to name something about the table's convergence. Eight or nine players are now saying "no target, I'd abstain." That's individually reasonable, but consider the mechanic: if town abstains as a block, the vote produces no elimination and no named votes. Mafia also gets to abstain or throw a safe vote with zero exposure. The uniformity of our agreement means the voting record we all say we'll use tomorrow is the record we're currently declining to create.

I'm not arguing we should lynch on no information — I agree with everyone who said that. I'm arguing we should be honest that abstention gives us behavioral reads only, not voting patterns, and Day 2 starts with the same vacuum we're in now.

Zara, direct question on a specific point: you pushed back on Elena's influence early, she corrected herself, and you've been quiet since. Do you think the table's consensus toward abstention is genuinely reasoned, or is it the path of least resistance — nobody wanting to be first to name a target?

Lucia, I think the abstention consensus is partly reasoned and partly the path of least resistance. People have explained why they don't want a low-information elimination, but the repeated insistence on a contradiction or a backed check risks setting the bar too high: mafia can be consistent, as Leo said.

I still don't have a target I can justify eliminating today. An all-abstain vote would give us little voting information, though the discussion itself remains a record. Tomorrow I want us to compare actual reads and alternatives, not treat abstention as automatically virtuous or a change of mind as automatically suspicious. And we should remember that eliminated roles aren't revealed, so an outcome alone won't tell us whether a voting bloc was right.

This is my third and final turn, so I'll close my position out cleanly.

First, Leo's pattern from earlier — arguing against an elimination and then voting for it without explaining what changed — is exactly the kind of testable record I said I'd vote on. I'd add one caveat he already named: I'd compare it against the alternatives before treating it as sufficient, since someone can legitimately update under new argument. The distinguishing feature is the missing explanation, not the change of mind itself.

Second, Lucia's warning about uniform abstention is correct and I want to concede it fully: if all of us abstain, we create no voting record, and Day 2 starts in the same vacuum. But I won't let that pressure me into spending a body to manufacture data — a manufactured record built on a coin-flip lynch teaches us mostly that we'll trade a villager for information. So here is my concrete commitment instead, per my own standard about testable future behavior: today I abstain. Tomorrow, if nobody has produced a contradiction or a backed claim, I will not abstain by default. I'll vote based on the discussion record — who updated honestly under challenge, who deflected, who set standards and then quietly dropped them — even if that record is imperfect. I'd rather cast an imperfect named vote tomorrow than hide behind abstention twice.

My status for the record, unchanged: I'm not claiming a role, I have no result, and I have no lynch target today. Nobody has met the table's standard, and I don't expect anyone to.

Amara, one direct question on a specific point, because it decides how I read you tomorrow: you stated you're a villager and that you support abstaining unless concrete evidence emerges. Is that abstention unconditional — meaning you'll abstain tomorrow too if no contradiction or backed claim appears — or is there a threshold of accumulated reads at which you'd name someone? If it's unconditional, that's a commitment I'll hold you to; if it's a threshold, tell me what's on it.

Isha, direct answer: my support for abstaining today is definitely not unconditional, and I will not treat abstention as a default for Day 2.

Day 1 is unique because there is literally zero prior game history—no night deaths, no investigation checks, no voting data, and no defense arguments under real pressure. In that vacuum, eliminating someone is essentially a coin toss that disproportionately damages town numbers. That is why abstaining today is tactical caution, not a long-term doctrine.

Tomorrow, however, the state of the board changes. We will have the result of Night 1—whether someone was eliminated or saved, potential investigative information if a power role chooses to disclose, and the public record of who voted or abstained today. My threshold for Day 2 does not require a smoking-gun contradiction or a verified detective report. It rests on comparative behavior: evaluating who pushed narratives that diverted attention, whose tone or logic shifted once night results arrived, and who attempted to hide behind an easy consensus. If we wait for absolute certainty or blatant self-contradictions, competent mafia will simply coast on smooth, consistent play.

So to be completely clear: I support abstaining today because guessing blind hurts town. Tomorrow, I expect to take a stand and cast a named vote based on the accumulated discussion and behavioral shifts, even if that evidence is circumstantial.

This is my third and final turn, so I'll close my Day 1 position cleanly.

The table has converged on abstaining today, and individually every reason given is sound — no results, no contradictions, no backed claims. I'll restate my one concern for the last time: if all nine of us abstain, the voting record we keep promising to analyze tomorrow doesn't exist. Behavioral reads from discussion alone are weaker than the record we'd get from actual votes, and that trade-off is being made knowingly by everyone here. I'd rather we name it than discover it.

What's been banked that matters: Elena publicly narrowed her own rule. Maya answered Leo's challenge on early claims and conceded a narrow point honestly. Isha revised her report-soon position under Leo's counterargument and corrected her own error about Leo's silence. Amara clarified her abstention is conditional with a Day 2 threshold. Leo gave us the sharpest testable pattern: argue against an elimination, then vote for it without explaining what changed. These are tomorrow's benchmarks.

My position for the record: abstain today, no target, no blame. Day 2 I vote on who honors or breaks their commitments — not on talk volume, not on who spoke first.

Felix, one direct question, because it's the last thing I'll ask before the vote: you said the details around a claim matter more than the claim itself, and you'd rather hear the remaining voices before locking a vote. Everyone has now spoken. Has hearing the full table changed where you land on abstaining today, or does your "no target" still hold? I want your explicit position on the vote, not just on the reads.

Lucia, direct answer: hearing the full table has not changed where I land on today's vote. I still have no night result, no check, no role claim beyond saying I have nothing concrete to report, and I have not seen a contradiction or backed claim that would justify a body. I abstain today.

I agree with your point that an all-abstain vote leaves us without a named voting record, and I won't pretend that cost is zero. But manufacturing a record by spending a coin-flip lynch is worse; it teaches us mostly that town will trade a villager for thin data. My position is the same as it was when you asked: details around claims and commitments matter more than the claim or silence itself, and I will state anything concrete plainly if I get it. Nobody has met that standard today, so I assign no blame and name no target.

Kenji here, with my third and final speaking turn. I have no role claim, no check, and no lynch target today, so I am abstaining along with the table's emerging consensus.

Lucia's point deserves a direct answer. An all-abstain vote gives us no named voting record, and I agree that is a real cost. But I agree with Isha and Felix that spending a body on a coin flip would teach town the wrong lesson. The better use of today is to bank the commitments people have made in public, since they are the most testable things we have.

Here is my standard for tomorrow, so everyone can hold me to it. If nobody has produced a check or a contradiction by then, I will vote on the strength of the discussion record: who updated honestly under challenge, who set a standard and then quietly dropped it, and who pushed the conversation toward a target without giving reasons. I will name the player I think best fits that record and explain why. I will not abstain by default twice, as Isha said.

I also want to put one caution on the record. Leo's pattern of arguing against an elimination and then voting for it without explanation is a good test, but it should be applied to the final vote, not to the discussion alone. Several players have changed their positions today with reasons attached, and those updates should count as honest revision unless the reasons are missing.

For the power holders: I agree with Leo that timing should depend on the result and the risk. I do not think anyone should be pushed to claim on Day 1, and I would rather the detective and doctor act on their own judgment than on pressure from this table.

So my position is simple. No target today, no blame, and a commitment to a named vote tomorrow based on commitments kept or broken.
Voting begins.
The votes are revealed.
All players abstained. Nobody is eliminated.
Night begins.
Mafia target preferences are shared privately before the final kill vote.
Zara is not mafia.
Elena was eliminated.
Day 2 begins.

Elena's elimination is the first hard fact of this game, and I want to be precise about what it proves. Mafia only kill town players at night. Elena was killed at night. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
